title: The Future of Evals: From LLM as a Judge to Agent as a Judge — Aparna Dhinakaran, Arize AI

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is the evolution of evaluation methodology from deterministic checks through LLM-as-a-judge to agent-as-a-judge. It discusses eval design, judging approaches, testing methodology for AI agents, and quantitative benchmarks of eval adoption across teams. The inclusion criteria 'Primary focus is evaluation design, benchmarks, judges, or testing methodology' is directly satisfied.

secondary.label: Observability, Reliability & LLMOps
secondary.rationale: The talk discusses online evals on production traces, Arize's Signal product reading production traces to discover failure patterns, and the role of production monitoring in fueling continual learning loops. This aligns with the observability focus on tracing, quality monitoring, and operating LLM systems.

secondary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
secondary.rationale: Agent-as-a-judge is itself an agent architecture pattern where an agent evaluates another agent. The talk also traces how agent architectures evolved from prompt-response to multi-step loops with tool calls, reasoning, and sub-agents, creating new failure classes that drove the need for evolved evals.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Arize is a developer platform for evaluation and observability, and the talk is delivered at the AI Engineer conference to a developer audience focused on building and evaluating AI systems.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The evaluation methodology discussed—deterministic checks, LLM-as-a-judge, agent-as-a-judge—is cross-domain and applicable to any AI agent system regardless of vertical.

summary: Aparna Dhinakaran, co-founder and CPO of Arize AI, presents the case that evaluation methods must evolve alongside the agents they assess. Arize processes over 100 million evals monthly, with average teams running about 12 eval jobs and top teams exceeding 3,800 evaluators. The talk traces an arc: in 2023, agents were essentially prompt-response systems; by 2024, frontier models added tool calls, reasoning, deep research, and long-horizon sub-agent loops. Each capability increase produced fundamentally new—not merely harder—failure modes that prior eval approaches could not detect. Arize experienced this firsthand with their own agent Alex, which gained longer memory, dynamic UI generation, and cross-trace search but exhibited failures such as forgetting context, not recognizing task completion, and getting stuck in loops. Classical LLM-as-a-judge evals with fixed rubrics could not capture these failure types because every user interaction produced a different trajectory. This led to the concept of agent-as-a-judge: adaptive, dynamic analysis that discovers patterns a fixed rubric would miss. Dhinakaran positions this as a third tool complementing, not replacing, deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge. Arize released Signal, a long-running agent that reads production traces, discovers subtle failure patterns such as repeated tool calls or inefficient trajectories, and can open pull requests with proposed fixes. The talk closes by inviting attendees to demos and the evals track sessions.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a coherent progression from problem to solution: the capability jump failure taxonomy explains why prior evaluation methods fail as agents evolve; deterministic checks, LLM-as-a-judge, and fixed rubric scoring represent the current state of practice that cannot capture non-deterministic trajectory failures; agent-as-a-judge and adaptive dynamic analysis represent the proposed evolution; production trace evaluation and trajectory analysis define the operational substrate on which agent-as-a-judge operates; and automated pull request generation with continual learning loops close the feedback cycle from failure discovery to system improvement. Understanding them together gives engineers a complete mental model for building evaluation pipelines that keep pace with agent capabilities—each concept is a necessary piece of the argument that evaluation architecture must evolve in lockstep with agent architecture.
temporalContext: The video was published on July 24, 2026, at the AI Engineer conference. Research was conducted as of August 22, 2026. In the intervening month, two significant events occurred: Arize AI was acquired by Dynatrace for $915M (announced August 13, 2026), and Signal was officially launched on July 29, 2026, five days after the video's publication. The talk reflects the state of agent evaluation practice in mid-2026, when agent-as-a-judge was emerging from research into production stacks and the industry was beginning to grapple with evaluation of multi-step, tool-calling, sub-agent-equipped systems.
takeaways: Evals must evolve as fast as the agents they grade; capability jumps create fundamentally new, not just harder, failure modes.
The arc runs from deterministic checks to LLM-as-a-judge to agent-as-a-judge; most teams today use only the first two but the future requires all three.
Arize runs over 100 million evals monthly; average teams run ~12 eval jobs, top teams exceed 3,800 evaluators.
Agent as a judge provides adaptive dynamic analysis, unlike LLM-as-a-judge's fixed rubric, detecting failures you would never think to write a check for.
Arize's own agent Alex exhibited failures—forgetting context, stuck loops, not knowing task completion—that classical LLM-as-a-judge could not catch.
The progression from 2023 (prompt answering) to 2024 (tool calls, reasoning, deep research, sub-agent loops) each represented a fundamentally different type of problem.
Arize released Signal, a long-running agent that reads traces, discovers issue patterns, and can open PRs with fixes.
Online evals on production traces are what help teams catch failures and fuel continual learning loops.

concepts.name: Deterministic evaluation checks
concepts.explanation: Code-based tests that verify specific properties of LLM outputs using predefined assertions, forming the foundational evaluation layer.
concepts.importance: The baseline evaluation layer that catches known, predictable failures but cannot handle non-deterministic agent trajectories.

concepts.name: LLM-as-a-judge
concepts.explanation: Using an LLM with a fixed rubric to evaluate the quality of another model's output, the second evaluation stage that handles nuanced but pre-defined quality criteria.
concepts.importance: The dominant method for qualitative evaluation of LLM outputs, but limited by fixed rubrics that cannot capture dynamic agent failure patterns.

concepts.name: Agent-as-a-judge
concepts.explanation: Using an adaptive agent to evaluate another agent's behavior, providing dynamic analysis that discovers failure patterns a fixed rubric would miss, such as inefficient tool-call loops or forgotten context.
concepts.importance: The third and newest evaluation paradigm that addresses the failure modes of non-deterministic, multi-step agent trajectories that earlier methods cannot detect.

concepts.name: Fixed rubric scoring
concepts.explanation: Pre-defined evaluation criteria applied uniformly across all outputs, which fails when agent trajectories are non-deterministic and user-dependent, producing a different path each time.
concepts.importance: Understanding its limitations is key to recognizing why agent-as-a-judge and adaptive analysis are needed.

concepts.name: Adaptive dynamic analysis
concepts.explanation: Evaluation that adaptively inspects agent traces to discover unknown failure patterns without pre-written rubrics, the core mechanism distinguishing agent-as-a-judge from LLM-as-a-judge.
concepts.importance: The distinguishing capability that separates agent-as-a-judge from LLM-as-a-judge, enabling discovery of failure types engineers would never think to write a check for.

concepts.name: Agent failure modes
concepts.explanation: Classes of failures specific to multi-step agent systems including stuck tool-call loops, forgotten context across steps, and unrecognized task completion, which classical eval methods cannot detect.
concepts.importance: Defines the problem space that motivates the entire evolution of evaluation methods from deterministic through LLM-as-a-judge to agent-as-a-judge.

concepts.name: Trajectory analysis
concepts.explanation: Examining the full multi-step execution path of an agent rather than just its final output, necessary because failures occur mid-trajectory and are invisible to output-only evaluation.
concepts.importance: The analytical substrate that agent-as-a-judge operates on to discover failure patterns across the entire agent execution path.

concepts.name: Long-horizon sub-agent loops
concepts.explanation: Agent architectures where sub-agents handle delegated sub-tasks over extended execution horizons, creating complex multi-step trajectories that are difficult to evaluate with traditional methods.
concepts.importance: Represents the frontier of agent complexity that drives the need for evolved evaluation approaches beyond fixed rubrics.

concepts.name: Capability jump failure taxonomy
concepts.explanation: The insight that each agent capability increase (prompt answering to tool calls to reasoning to sub-agents) creates fundamentally different—not merely harder—failure modes, requiring qualitatively new evaluation approaches.
concepts.importance: The core argument for why evaluation methods must evolve rather than scale, framing the talk's central thesis.

concepts.name: Tool-call loop failures
concepts.explanation: Agent behavior patterns where iterative tool calls become inefficient or stuck, a failure mode detectable by agent-as-a-judge but invisible to fixed rubrics and deterministic checks.
concepts.importance: A concrete failure pattern that demonstrates the value of adaptive evaluation over fixed rubrics, used as a motivating example for Signal.

concepts.name: Evaluation pipeline architecture
concepts.explanation: Layering three complementary evaluation strategies—deterministic checks, LLM-as-a-judge, and agent-as-a-judge—in a combined pipeline rather than relying on any single method, so that each layer catches failure classes the others miss.
concepts.importance: Defines the architectural pattern for combining multiple evaluation methods in production AI systems, which is the talk's central engineering recommendation.

concepts.name: Production trace evaluation
concepts.explanation: Running evaluations on live production traces rather than offline test datasets, enabling teams to catch real-world failures and fuel continual learning loops.
concepts.importance: Connects evaluation to operations by using production data as the evaluation substrate, which is how teams discover trajectory-level failures invisible in offline tests.

concepts.name: Automated pull request generation
concepts.explanation: Signal's capability to automatically open pull requests with proposed code fixes based on discovered failure patterns in production traces, bridging evaluation and code remediation.
concepts.importance: Closes the loop between evaluation and code fix, reducing manual triage overhead and demonstrating a concrete engineering workflow for agent-as-a-judge.

concepts.name: Continual learning loops
concepts.explanation: Using online evaluation results from production traces to iteratively improve agent systems, creating a feedback loop between evaluation and deployment so that production failures become new test cases.
concepts.importance: Establishes the operational feedback cycle that turns production failures into system improvements, the connective tissue between eval and operations.

concepts.name: Evaluation scaling metrics
concepts.explanation: Quantitative benchmarks showing the range of evaluation adoption across teams: average teams run ~12 eval jobs while top teams exceed 3,800 evaluators, across 100M+ monthly evals processed by Arize.
concepts.importance: Provides concrete benchmarks for engineering teams to assess their evaluation maturity and understand the gap between average and top-tier practices.

organization.name: Arize AI
organization.summary: Arize AI is an AI engineering platform for teams shipping reliable AI agents and LLM applications, headquartered in San Francisco, California. Founded in 2020 by Jason Lopatecki (CEO) and Aparna Dhinakaran (CPO), Arize provides AI observability, evaluation, and continuous improvement tooling. Its products include Arize AX (managed AI engineering platform with Signal, Managed Agents, and evaluation capabilities), Phoenix (open-source observability and evaluation), and OpenInference (open standard for GenAI observability). The company processes over 100 million evals monthly and raised $70M in Series C funding in February 2025, bringing total funding to $131M. On August 13, 2026, Dynatrace announced a definitive agreement to acquire Arize for $915M. The video's speaker, Aparna Dhinakaran, is co-founder and CPO.
organization.status: Definitive acquisition agreement signed with Dynatrace ($915M), announced August 13, 2026; transaction pending close

technologies.label: Agent-as-a-judge evaluation methodology
technologies.summary: Agent-as-a-judge is an evaluation technique where an adaptive agent dynamically analyzes another agent's execution trajectories to discover failure patterns that fixed rubrics and deterministic checks cannot detect. Unlike LLM-as-a-judge, which applies pre-defined criteria uniformly, agent-as-a-judge adapts its analysis to each trajectory, discovering unknown failure types such as stuck tool-call loops, forgotten context, or unrecognized task completion. Dhinakaran positions it as a third evaluation layer complementing—not replacing—deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge, arguing that as agents gained tool calls, reasoning, deep research, and sub-agent loops from 2023 to 2024, each capability jump created fundamentally new failure classes requiring qualitatively new evaluation approaches.
technologies.role: Central thesis and primary technology presented by the speaker; the talk argues for its adoption as a third evaluation layer alongside deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge

technologies.label: Arize Signal managed evaluation agent
technologies.summary: Signal is Arize AI's managed agent implementation of agent-as-a-judge, built into the Arize AX platform. It continuously reviews production traces, surfaces ranked issues with evidence and root cause analysis, and can carry investigations into the codebase to open pull requests with proposed fixes. In the talk, Dhinakaran presents Signal as the concrete product realization of the agent-as-a-judge methodology, demonstrating how adaptive evaluation can discover failure patterns such as repeated tool calls or inefficient trajectories that fixed rubrics miss.
technologies.role: Featured product demonstration of agent-as-a-judge; shown reading traces, discovering failure patterns, and opening PRs with fixes

technologies.label: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
technologies.summary: LLM-as-a-judge is the evaluation technique where an LLM with a fixed rubric scores another model's output. It represents the second stage in the three-stage evaluation evolution discussed in the talk, handling nuanced quality assessment beyond what deterministic checks can cover. However, its fixed rubric approach cannot capture non-deterministic agent trajectory failures—such as stuck tool-call loops, forgotten context, or unrecognized task completion—motivating the need for agent-as-a-judge. Dhinakaran notes most teams today use deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge but lack the third agent-as-a-judge layer.
technologies.role: Discussed as the current standard evaluation method that agent-as-a-judge complements; its fixed-rubric limitations motivate the talk's central thesis for a three-stage eval evolution

technologies.label: Arize AX evaluation and observability platform
technologies.summary: Arize AX is Arize AI's managed AI engineering platform providing observability, evaluation, and guardrails for AI teams. It processes over 100 million evals monthly, with average teams running about 12 eval jobs and top teams exceeding 3,800 evaluators. The platform includes Signal as a built-in managed agent and serves as the operational substrate for the evaluation methodology discussed in the talk, enabling production trace evaluation and continual learning loops. Arize was acquired by Dynatrace for $915M on August 13, 2026, approximately three weeks after the video was published.
technologies.role: Platform context for the evaluation methodology and Signal product; Arize's eval infrastructure processing 100M+ monthly evals across teams with varying eval maturity
